lead: This unit explains how real fluids lose energy in pipes and how to compute head loss, pressure drop and flow split. After it you can classify pipe flow with Reynolds number, apply Hagen-Poiseuille and Darcy-Weisbach equations, read a Moody chart, add minor losses, draw HGL and TEL, solve series and parallel pipe systems, and estimate water-hammer pressure and siphon limits.
about: Unit 4 is about energy loss and pressure change when a real fluid moves through pipes. Chapter 4.1 uses Reynolds' dye experiment to separate laminar from turbulent flow. 4.2 gives the Hagen-Poiseuille equation for laminar pipe flow. 4.3 introduces Darcy-Weisbach head loss and the friction factor, and 4.4 shows how the Moody diagram supplies that factor for turbulent flow. 4.5 adds minor losses at fittings. 4.6 draws the hydraulic gradient and total energy lines. 4.7 combines pipes in series and parallel into equivalent pipes. 4.8 closes with water hammer and siphons. The chapters build in that order: classify the flow, compute friction, add fittings, then read the system head.

chapters.idea: A dye streak in a glass pipe changes from a straight line to a blurred cloud as the Reynolds number crosses the critical range, separating laminar from turbulent flow.
chapters.depth: Describe Reynolds' apparatus: constant-head tank, dye reservoir, glass tube, control valve. Define Re = ρVD/μ = VD/ν. Here ρ is density in kg/m³, V is mean velocity in m/s, D is pipe diameter in m, μ is dynamic viscosity in Pa·s, and ν is kinematic viscosity in m²/s. State common textbook critical values: lower critical Re ≈ 2000 and upper critical Re ≈ 4000 for pipe flow. Laminar below, transitional between, turbulent above. Explain dye behaviour and the difference in velocity profiles. Some syllabi call Re the Reynolds number and the in-between zone the critical zone. Do not derive pipe friction.

figure.title: Reynolds experiment
figure.aria: A constant-head tank sends water through a glass tube where dye is injected; a valve controls flow into a measuring jar.

chapters.example: Water (ν = 1.0×10⁻⁶ m²/s) flows through a 50 mm diameter glass pipe. The mean velocity is 0.06 m/s. Find Re and classify the flow. Repeat for 0.20 m/s. For 0.06 m/s, Re = 0.06 × 0.05 / 1.0×10⁻⁶ = 3000, so the flow is transitional. For 0.20 m/s, Re = 0.20 × 0.05 / 1.0×10⁻⁶ = 10000, so the flow is turbulent.
chapters.trap: Using pipe radius in place of diameter. Re is dimensionless, so all lengths must use the same unit.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 viscosity and density; Unit 2 laminar and turbulent classification.
chapters.leave: Friction factor and head loss to 4.3; boundary-layer transition to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: In steady laminar flow through a circular pipe, the velocity profile is a paraboloid and discharge varies as the fourth power of diameter.
chapters.depth: Derive from a force balance on a cylinder of fluid: τ = (Δp/L)(r/2). Integrate the shear relation to get the parabolic profile. Give Hagen-Poiseuille results: Q = π Δp D⁴/(128 μ L) and Δp = 32 μ L V/D². Head loss is h_f = 32 μ L V/(ρgD²) = 128 ν L Q/(πgD⁴). Velocity is u(r) = 2V[1 − (r/R)²], where V = Q/(πD²/4) is mean velocity and R = D/2. Wall shear is τ_w = Δp D/(4L). State assumptions: steady, laminar, incompressible, fully developed, no slip, horizontal pipe. Mention the capillary-tube viscometer.

figure.aria: A parabolic curve falls from twice the mean velocity at the pipe centre to zero velocity at the wall.

chapters.example: Oil (μ = 0.10 Pa·s, ρ = 900 kg/m³) flows through a 20 mm diameter, 10 m long horizontal pipe at Q = 1.0×10⁻⁵ m³/s. Check that the flow is laminar, then find the pressure drop and head loss. Area = π(0.02)²/4 = 3.142×10⁻⁴ m², so V = 0.0318 m/s and Re = 900 × 0.0318 × 0.02 / 0.10 = 5.73, laminar. Δp = 128 μ L Q/(πD⁴) = 2547 Pa. h_f = Δp/(ρg) = 2547/(900 × 9.81) = 0.288 m.
chapters.trap: Using D instead of R in u(r). Q varies as D⁴, so a 10% diameter error gives about a 46% discharge error.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 viscosity; Unit 2 continuity and laminar flow; Unit 3 Bernoulli for head.
chapters.leave: Turbulent velocity profiles and friction factor to 4.3 and 4.4; non-circular ducts to Unit 5 or later.

chapters.idea: The Darcy-Weisbach equation turns friction into a head loss proportional to velocity head, pipe length and a friction factor.
chapters.depth: Define the Darcy friction factor f, also called the Darcy-Weisbach friction factor. h_f = f (L/D)(V²/(2g)). Here L is pipe length in m, D is diameter in m, V is mean velocity in m/s, and g = 9.81 m/s². For laminar flow, f = 64/Re. For turbulent flow, f depends on Re and relative roughness ε/D; give the Colebrook-White equation. Warn that the Fanning friction factor f_F equals f/4. Give Chezy's equation V = C√(R_h S), where C is Chezy coefficient, R_h is hydraulic radius and S is slope; for a full pipe, f = 8g/C². Use Moody diagram in 4.4.

series.name: h_f for L=50 m, D=0.1 m, f=0.02

figure.aria: A rising parabola shows head loss increasing with the square of mean velocity for fixed length, diameter and friction factor.

chapters.example: Water flows at V = 2.0 m/s through a 100 mm diameter, 50 m long pipe. Take f = 0.02. Find the head loss and pressure drop. h_f = f (L/D)(V²/(2g)) = 0.02 × (50/0.1) × (2.0²/(2 × 9.81)) = 2.04 m. Δp = ρg h_f = 1000 × 9.81 × 2.04 = 20.0 kPa.
chapters.trap: Mixing the Darcy friction factor with the Fanning friction factor. Also, f = 64/Re is only for laminar flow.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 viscosity and density; Unit 2 Reynolds number; 4.2 laminar pipe flow.
chapters.leave: Reading f from the Moody diagram to 4.4; minor losses to 4.5.

chapters.idea: The Moody diagram stores turbulent friction factors so that Re and relative roughness give f without solving the Colebrook equation by hand.
chapters.depth: A Moody diagram plots f against Re on log-log axes for curves of relative roughness ε/D. Describe regions: laminar line f = 64/Re; critical zone; smooth-pipe turbulent curve; transitionally rough zone; fully rough zone where f is almost constant. Reading steps: compute Re, compute ε/D, enter the chart, read f. Give the Colebrook-White equation and the Haaland approximation. Use the chart only for turbulent pipe friction. Some syllabi call it Moody's chart or Moody chart.

figure.aria: Two falling curves show friction factor against Reynolds number for a smooth pipe and for relative roughness 0.002.

chapters.example: Water flows at V = 1.5 m/s through a 200 mm diameter, 100 m long pipe. Re = 1×10⁵ and ε/D = 0.002. Read f from a Moody diagram, then find h_f. The chart gives f ≈ 0.025. h_f = f (L/D)(V²/(2g)) = 0.025 × (100/0.2) × (1.5²/(2 × 9.81)) = 1.43 m.
chapters.trap: Reading ε as roughness height in mm instead of ε/D. Also, do not use the laminar straight line for turbulent flow.
chapters.leave: Derivation of Colebrook-White and roughness tables to a design handbook; minor-loss coefficients to 4.5.

chapters.idea: A real pipe system loses head in straight pipe friction and also at every fitting, bend, valve and entrance.
chapters.depth: Major loss is the Darcy-Weisbach friction loss over straight pipe. Minor loss is h_m = K V²/(2g), where K is a dimensionless loss coefficient and V is the local mean velocity. Cover entrance (K ≈ 0.5), exit (K = 1.0), sudden contraction, sudden expansion, bend, elbow and valve. For sudden expansion, h = (V₁ − V₂)²/(2g). Equivalent length is L_e = K D/f. Minor losses are often ignored when L/D is large, but not when the pipe is short. Total head loss = Σ major + Σ minor.

figure.title: Losses along a pipeline
figure.aria: A pipeline block diagram shows the tank, entrance, straight pipe, elbows, valve and exit, each with its loss coefficient.

chapters.example: A 50 mm diameter pipe is 20 m long, carries water at V = 1.2 m/s, and has f = 0.03. The fittings are one entrance K = 0.5, two elbows each K = 0.9, one valve K = 2.5 and one exit K = 1.0. Find the total head loss. V²/(2g) = 1.2²/(2 × 9.81) = 0.0734 m. Major loss = 0.03 × (20/0.05) × 0.0734 = 0.881 m. ΣK = 0.5 + 1.8 + 2.5 + 1.0 = 5.8, so minor loss = 5.8 × 0.0734 = 0.426 m. Total loss = 1.307 m.
chapters.trap: Adding minor-loss K values but using a different velocity for each fitting. Also, minor losses are not always small.
chapters.leave: Detailed manufacturer K values to a design handbook; equivalent pipe systems to 4.7.

chapters.idea: The total energy line falls by every head loss, while the hydraulic gradient line sits one velocity head below it.
chapters.depth: Define total head H = z + p/(ρg) + V²/(2g) and piezometric head h = z + p/(ρg). Here z is elevation in m and p is gauge pressure in Pa. TEL plots H; HGL plots h. Their vertical gap is V²/(2g). Both fall in the flow direction because of losses. TEL always falls without a pump; HGL can rise in a diffuser because velocity head falls. Slope of TEL is h_f/L. At a reservoir surface, TEL = HGL = surface elevation. At a free outlet, p = 0 gauge.

figure.aria: Two falling parallel lines show total energy and hydraulic gradient between sections A and B, with TEL above HGL by the velocity head.

chapters.example: Water flows at V = 1.5 m/s in a 100 mm pipe. At section A, z = 5.0 m and p = 40 kPa. At section B, 30 m downstream, z = 5.5 m and p = 30 kPa. Find HGL and TEL at A and B, and the head loss between them. At A: p/(ρg) = 40000/(1000 × 9.81) = 4.077 m, HGL = 9.077 m, velocity head = 1.5²/(2 × 9.81) = 0.115 m, TEL = 9.192 m. At B: p/(ρg) = 30000/(1000 × 9.81) = 3.058 m, HGL = 8.558 m, TEL = 8.673 m. Head loss = 9.192 − 8.673 = 0.519 m.
chapters.trap: Drawing HGL above TEL, or forgetting that p in the head formula is gauge pressure.
chapters.prereq: Unit 3 Bernoulli equation; 4.5 major and minor losses.
chapters.leave: Pump and turbine head changes to Units 6 and 7; pipe-network analysis to 4.7.

chapters.idea: Pipe systems reduce to one equivalent pipe by using the rules that series pipes share discharge and parallel pipes share head loss.
chapters.depth: Series: same discharge Q; head losses add; total head H = Σ h_fi. For the same f and an equivalent diameter D_e, L_e/D_e⁵ = Σ L_i/D_i⁵. Parallel: same head loss across each branch; discharges add Q = Σ Q_i. For the same f, Q_i ∝ √(D_i⁵/L_i). For parallel pipes of equal D and f, 1/√L_e = Σ 1/√L_i. General method: write the head-loss equation for each branch and solve. An equivalent pipe gives the same Q for the same total head loss.

figure.title: Two parallel pipes
figure.aria: Two pipes of different lengths leave node A and join at node B, showing a parallel pipe system.

chapters.example: Two parallel pipes connect the same two nodes. Pipe 1: L₁ = 100 m, D₁ = 0.10 m, f = 0.02. Pipe 2: L₂ = 200 m, D₂ = 0.10 m, f = 0.02. Total flow is Q = 0.03 m³/s. Find the flow in each pipe and the equivalent length at D = 0.10 m. Equal head loss gives Q₁/Q₂ = √(L₂/L₁) = √2 = 1.414. Thus Q₁ = 0.0176 m³/s and Q₂ = 0.0124 m³/s. Equivalent length: 1/√L_e = 1/√100 + 1/√200, so L_e = 34.3 m.
chapters.trap: In series, adding discharges; in parallel, adding head losses. Also, series equivalent length uses D⁵, not a simple length sum.
chapters.leave: Complex looped networks and Hardy Cross method to a later design course; pump combinations to Unit 7.

chapters.idea: A fast valve closure sends a pressure wave through a pipe, while a siphon uses low pressure at a crest to lift water over an obstacle.
chapters.depth: Water hammer: a sudden velocity change creates a pressure surge. For a thin-walled pipe, wave speed a = √(K/ρ) / √(1 + K D/(E t)), where K is bulk modulus, E is pipe modulus, D is diameter and t is wall thickness. Rapid closure occurs when closure time T_c < 2L/a. The Joukowsky pressure rise is Δp = ρaV. Slow closure gives a smaller rise. Surge tanks and air vessels reduce the surge. Siphon: a pipe rises above the source level and discharges lower; flow is driven by gravity. Pressure at the crest is below atmospheric. Maximum crest height is limited by vapour pressure and cavitation. A siphon must be primed. Some syllabi spell siphon as syphon.

figure.title: Siphon
figure.aria: A siphon pipe leaves an upper reservoir, rises to a low-pressure crest and falls to a lower reservoir.

chapters.example: A steel pipe has D = 0.20 m, wall thickness t = 5 mm, E = 200 GPa and K = 2.2 GPa. Water flows at V = 2.0 m/s. A valve closes rapidly. Find the wave speed and pressure rise. Take ρ = 1000 kg/m³. K/ρ = 2.2×10⁶ m²/s², so √(K/ρ) = 1483 m/s. K D/(E t) = (2.2×10⁹ × 0.20)/(200×10⁹ × 0.005) = 0.44. a = 1483/√1.44 = 1236 m/s. Δp = ρaV = 1000 × 1236 × 2.0 = 2.47×10⁶ Pa = 2.47 MPa.
chapters.trap: Using the Joukowsky pressure rise for slow closure. Also, a siphon crest can cavitate if pressure falls below vapour pressure.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 bulk modulus; Unit 3 Bernoulli; 4.6 HGL and TEL.
chapters.leave: Surge-tank sizing and pipe stress to later design courses; pump cavitation to Unit 7.
